parole.significato: Forming nouns with the sense of "action or result of Xing" or, more rarely, "action related to X".
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -age, from Old French -age, from Latin -āticum, greatly extended from words like rivage and voyage.

parole.significato: forms the first-person singular past historic indicative form of an -er verb
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āvī.

parole.significato: used to form names of orchards or places where trees/plants are grown
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēta, plural of -ētum. Cognate to Italian -eta and -eto.

parole.significato: Forming masculine nouns from verbs and nouns, having the sense of ‘tool, object for a specific purpose’.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āculum. Doublet of -acle, which is borrowed from Latin -āculum.

parole.significato: forms feminine nouns having a colloquial or pejorative meaning, or indicating the means or result of an action

parole.significato: forms verbs with frequentative effect, often somewhat pejorative
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āculāre.

parole.significato: suffix used to form noun (uppercase) demonyms
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ain, from Old French -ain, from Latin -ānus, whence also French -an and -ien.
Inherited from Middle French -ain, from Latin -āneus, whence also French -ané.

parole.significato: indicates approximation, suffixed to a number
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēna.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin -ārium, the accusative of -ārius; or (in the feminine) from -āria. Compare the inherited doublet of -ier/-ière.

parole.significato: forms the first-person and second-person singular imperfect indicative form of a verb
parole.testo: From Middle French -ois, from conflation of Latin -ēbās and -iēbas — originally second-, third-, and fourth-conjugation variants of -bās, which had been later generalized to all verbs.

parole.significato: forms feminine nouns of action from verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French -ison, inherited from Latin -ātiō. Compare the borrowed doublet -ation, and further the form -ison, from Latin -ītiō.

parole.significato: forms the third-person singular imperfect indicative form of a verb

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -al, from Old French -al, borrowed from Latin -ālis. Doublet of -el, which is inherited. The masculine plural in -x comes from the letter's usage as a ligature to abbreviate -us.
From Old French -ance, from Latin -antia. Compare Spanish -anza, -enza, Italian -anza, -enza, Portuguese -ança, -ença, Romanian -ință. Cognate to French -ence.

parole.significato: -ing; suffix denoting the gerund and present participle of a verb
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French -ant, from a merger of Latin -antem, -entem (present participle suffix) with Latin -andum, -endum (gerundive suffix). Compare Italian -ante, -ando; Spanish -ante, -ando.

Borrowed from Latin -archia, from Ancient Greek ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).

parole.significato: found in borrowed Latin past participles (sometimes nominalized)
parole.testo: Derived from Latin -ātus, -ātī (whence also English -ate, -ee). Doublet of -é (past participle suffix), which is inherited. See also the etymology at English -ate.

parole.significato: forms the noun denoting the result, product, object, or effect of the action expressed by a verb
parole.testo: Derived from Latin -ātum, -ātī (whence also English -ate, -atum), from the substantivized neuter singular of perfect passive participles in -ātus. Doublet of -é.

parole.significato: Used to indicate action, condition, result or effect; -ation

parole.significato: forms the feminine of nouns referring to people

Inherited from Old French -el, from Latin -ālis. Doublet of -al.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives or nouns denoting age and masculine nouns denoting anniversaries (-ennial) from numerals

Borrowed from Latin -entia. Compare Italian -enza, Portuguese -ença, -ência, Romanian -ință, -ență, Spanish -enza, -encia. Doublet of -ance, which is inherited.
Inherited from Latin -entem. Mostly confined to learned formations; inherited words tend to use the spelling -ant.

parole.significato: forms the third-person plural present indicative form of a verb
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ant, -ent, -iunt.

parole.significato: forms nouns indicating the person who exercises a particular activity

parole.significato: used to form feminine forms of nouns, especially ones with masculine counterparts in -eur
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin -ātrīcem, initially inherited as Old French -eriz; later changed to -eresse under the influence of -esse and superficial analysis as -eur + -esse. Doublet of -atrice, which was borrowed later.

parole.significato: forms the second-person singular present indicative form of a verb
parole.testo: From Latin -ās.

parole.significato: used to form nouns describing the condition of being something (-ness, -ity, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French -ece, from Latin -itia. The modern spelling is due to a phonetic merger with etymology 2; see below. Related to -ise.

parole.significato: forms masculine agent nouns from verbs (some of which are also used as adjectives)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -eur, from Old French -or / -eor / -eur, from Latin -tōrem and -ātōrem, from Proto-Italic *-tōr, from Proto-Indo-European *-tōr. Doublet of -ateur.
Inherited from Middle French -eur, from Old French -or, from Latin -ōrem, from Proto-Italic *-ōs, from Proto-Indo-European *-ōs.

parole.significato: forms adjectives with a comparative sense

parole.significato: forms the second-person plural indicative and imperative of several verb conjugations
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ātis (“second-person plural indicative present suffix for the first conjugation”). parole.significato: indicates a feminine noun, often an abstract one

parole.significato: forms nouns denoting where something or someone is from; -ian
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ien, from Old French -ien, from Latin -iānus, from -ānus. Doublet of -ain and -an.

parole.significato: forms the names of trees or bushes bearing a particular type of fruit
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ier, -er, from Old French -ier, -er, from Latin -ārium, the accusative of -ārius. Compare the borrowed doublet -aire.

parole.significato: -ive; forms adjectives denoting characteristics or qualities
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -if, from Old French -if, from Latin -īvus.

parole.significato: Suffix found in nouns naming members of Germanic tribes or dynasties.

Inherited from Middle French -ique, from Old French -ique, a learned borrowing from Latin -icus, from Proto-Italic *-ikos, from Proto-Indo-European *-ikos.

parole.significato: forms the infinitives of many verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -īre, the ending of the present active infinitive form of fourth conjugation verbs. Cognate with Spanish -ir, Italian -ire, Romanian -i and -î, etc.

parole.significato: forms the first-person singular present indicative of -ir verbs

Borrowed from Latin -isma, -ismus.

Borrowed from Latin -ista.

From Middle French -itude, borrowed from Latin -(i)tūdō.

parole.significato: A suffix forming infinitives of some verbs.

parole.significato: Suffix used to form adjectives matched to nouns ending in -ation (or its variants) and derived from a Latin verb.

parole.significato: Suffix used on verbs to form feminine nouns, generally referring to objects or tools used to do something.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -(āt)ōria(m), the feminine singular form of the above. Compare Italian -toia.

parole.significato: added to a noun to form a diminutive, or a depreciative form of that noun

parole.significato: forms diminutives of things, including some animals

From Latin -phila, from Ancient Greek φίλος (phílos, “dear, beloved”).

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -s, from Old French -s, from Latin -es, -is (second-person singular). parole.testo: Attested since the 11th century, from Old French -te, from Latin -ita, the feminine of the past participle ending -itus.

parole.significato: -ty (suffix used to form nouns, often denoting a quality or a property)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -té, from Old French -té, from Latin -itātem, or -tātem, accusative singular of -tās, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts. Compare the borrowed doublet -ité.

parole.significato: forms adjectives having the sense of ‘having quality of, being provided with’ (the root word)

parole.significato: forms the first-person plural past historic of -er verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -āvimus. The circumflex is by analogy with -âtes.

parole.significato: forms the second-person plural past historic of -er verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French -astes, from Latin -āstis, short counterpart to -āvistis.
Inherited from Old French -astre, from Latin -astrum. Cognate to Italian -astro.

parole.significato: forms the third-person plural past historic of -er verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -ārunt, contracted form of -āverunt.

parole.significato: forms the noun denoting the result, product, object, or effect of the action expressed by a verb
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ātum (second declension), from the substantivized neuter singular of perfect passive participles in -ātus. Doublet of -at (“result suffix”).

parole.significato: forms a feminine noun indicating a quantity or content measured by what the base noun denotes, often translatable as -f…

parole.significato: ending found in male names from Greek

parole.significato: from priestly authority, from divine office
parole.testo: From Latin ā dīvīnīs, from ab (“from”) and the ablative of dīvīna n pl (“sacred things”).

parole.significato: a latere (being sent by the pope to represent him personally in a temporary and important mission)
parole.testo: From Latin a latere (literally “from the [Pope's] side”).

parole.significato: A prefix forming words, especially verbs, that denote entering a state, making progress toward a goal, or the like.

parole.testo: From Middle French abiurer, abjurer, from Old French abjurer (“to reject or renounce (something) on oath”), borrowed from Latin abiūrāre (“to deny on oath, recant, renounce, repudiate, abjure”).
Borrowed from Latin (cāsus) ablātīvus (“ablative case, ablative”), from ablātus (“taken away”), from auferō (“to take away”).

parole.significato: to stop; to prevent; to hinder
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French empeechier, inherited from Latin impedicāre. Cognate with English impeach. Doublet of empiéger.

parole.significato: in (used to indicate space, also see usage notes)
parole.testo: From Middle French en, from Old French en, from Latin in, from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”).

parole.testo: From Latin inde (“thence”). Compare Catalan en, Italian ne.

parole.significato: to incur (to expose oneself to something inconvenient)
parole.testo: From en- + courir, calque of Latin incurrō.
From en- + dormir or Latin indormīre.

Inherited from Old French enfance, borrowed from Latin īnfāntia, from īnfāns (“unable to speak”).

parole.significato: child (someone who is not yet an adult)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French enfant, from Old French enfant, from Latin īnfantem.
Inherited from Old French enfer, from Latin īnfernus.

parole.significato: to set fire to, to set on fire
parole.testo: Latinized respelling of Old French enflamer, from Latin inflammāre. By surface analysis, en- + flamme + -er.
Inherited from Old French enfler, from Latin īnflāre.
Inherited from Middle French engendrer, from Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerāre.

parole.significato: any device, contraption or machinery, particularly a complex, dangerous or powerful one
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French engin m, from Old French engin m, from Latin ingenium n.

parole.significato: to order; to enjoin (someone à faire something)
parole.testo: First attested circa 1191 in Old French as anjoindre, from Latin injungere, iniungere, altered after joindre.

Inherited from Middle French enthousiasme, from Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós).

Inherited from Middle French entre, from Old French entre, inherited from Latin inter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”). Doublet of inter-, a borrowing.

parole.testo: Calque of Latin inter canem et lupum (“between a dog and a wolf”), because at that time in the day, one can't see the difference. Traditional sentiment, dating to antiquity (found in 2nd century CE texts), in French from the 18th century.
Calque of Latin inter vīvōs.

From Latin Ephthalītēs, from Ancient Greek Ἐφθαλίτης (Ephthalítēs).
From Old French errant, from Latin errantem.
Inherited from Old French erratique, borrowed from Latin erraticus.

parole.significato: way, inertia, movement through the water

From Old French errer, from Latin errāre.

parole.significato: error (a faulty process of thought that leads to conclusions out of agreement with reality)

Inherited from Middle French errone, from Latin errōneus (“vagrant, wrong”), from errō (“to go astray”).

Inherited from Latin exāmen. Doublet of examen.

Inherited from Old French pagien, païen, from Latin pāgānus (“rural, rustic; pagan”), from pāgus (“countryside”).

parole.significato: skin of a person or animal
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French peau, from Old French pel, from Latin pellem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).
Borrowed from Latin pectorālis. Doublet of poitrail.
Inherited from Old French peigne, from Latin pectinem.
Inherited from Old French paigner, from Latin pectināre.
Inherited from Middle French paindre, from Old French peindre, paindre, inherited from Latin pingere (“to paint”).

Inherited from Old French peine, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Cognate with Spanish pena, Italian pena, Portuguese pena. False friend of Spanish peine (“comb”).
Borrowed from Latin pellicula (“small skin or hide”).
From Latin pellicula.

From Old French pendeloche (“penis”) (apparently a hapax legomenon), from pendeler (“to dangle”) + -oche (suffix forming nouns from verbs), with the ending possibly influenced by breloque (“charm for a bracelet”). Clipping of Middle French funependule, a borrowing from Latin funependulus, from the ablative of funis + pendulus.

parole.significato: to think, reflect, concentrate one's mind on something
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French penser, from Old French penser, from Latin pēnsāre, whence also the doublet peser, as well as panser, originally an alternative spelling which acquired a special sense.
Inherited from Old French pension, panssion, borrowed from Latin pēnsiōnem (“payment, rent”), from pēnsus, the past participle of pendō (“weigh, pay”).
Borrowed from Latin pēnsum. Doublet of poids, which was inherited.

parole.significato: pentagon (a polygon with five sides and five angles)
parole.testo: From Latin pentagonus, which came from πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos). Morphologically penta- + -gone.
From Latin pentēcontarchia, from Ancient Greek πεντηκονταρχία (pentēkontarkhía). By surface analysis, pentécontarque + -ie.

parole.significato: pentecontarch (the commander of a platoon of fifty men)
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchus, from Ancient Greek πεντηκόνταρχος (pentēkóntarkhos, literally “commander of fifty”).
From Latin per-.

From Latin perfectus + -ible.

Learned borrowing from Latin perfidus.

From Latin perforātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin perforāre (“to bore or pierce through; to perforate”).

parole.significato: Pergamene (native or inhabitant of Pergamum) (usually male)
parole.testo: From Latin Pergamēnus, from Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós).
From Middle French permanant, permanent, from Latin permanentem (accusative of permanēns).

parole.significato: to permit, to allow (to grant permission or access)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French permettre, borrowed from Latin permittere, based on French mettre.
Borrowed from Latin permissiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Latin permūtātiō, from permūtāre.
From Latin permūtāre (“transform; exchange”) (Middle French: permuer/parmuer).
Inherited from Latin perna (“mussel”).

parole.significato: insidious (having a slow and discreet, but dangerous evolution)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin perniciōsus.
Borrowed from Latin perplexus, composed by per- + plexus, past participle of the verb plectere.

Inherited from Old French persil, peresil, perresil, inherited from Latin petroselīnum (possibly through a Vulgar Latin *petrosīnu, compare Sicilian pitrusinu and the Old French variant persin, later with the suffix -il; or through Early Medieval Latin petrosilio), itself from Ancient Greek πετροσέλ
From Perse + -ique, or borrowed from Latin Persicus (hence a doublet of pêche).
Borrowed from Latin persistere.
Inherited from Middle French personne, from Old French persone, presonne, from Latin persona, of unknown, perhaps Etruscan, origin.

Inherited from Middle French persuader, from Latin persuādeō (“to persuade”).
Learned borrowing from Latin persuāsiō.
From Latin Perseidēs. By surface analysis, Persée (“Perseus”) + -ide (“-id”)
From Latin Perseis. By surface analysis, Persée (“Perseus”) + -ide (“-id”)

parole.significato: perseverance (persistent determination to adhere to a course of action)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin persevērantia. By surface analysis, persévérer + -ance.
From Old French perseverer, borrowed from Latin persevērāre.
Inherited from Middle French perte, from Old French perte, from the feminine of Latin perditus. Compare Italian perdita and Spanish pérdida.

From Latin pertusus.

Learned borrowing from Latin perversiōnis.
Learned borrowing from Latin perversitās. Morphologically, from pervers + -ité.

parole.significato: to weigh (to have a weight of)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French peser, from Old French peser, from Classical Latin pēnsāre, whence also the doublet penser 'think'.

parole.significato: pessimism (general belief that bad things will happen)

Learned borrowing from Latin pestis (“plague; pest”).
Inherited from Old French pestilence, borrowed from Latin pestilentia.
Inherited from Middle French pet, from Old French pet, from Latin pēditum.

Inherited from Middle French peuple, from Old French pueple, semi-learned form of pueble, from earliest Old French poblo (9th c.), from Latin populus, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”). Doublet of people and pueblo.
Inherited from Middle French peur, from Old French peor, poür, from Latin pavōrem (“fear, fright”). Compare Catalan por and Italian paura.

From Latin phallobata, adapted form of phallobatēs, from Ancient Greek φαλλοβάτης (phallobátēs). By surface analysis, phallo- + -bate.

parole.testo: From Latin philosophaster. By surface analysis, philosophe + -âtre.

parole.significato: philter (a kind of potion, charm, or drug intended to make the drinker fall in love with the giver)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin philtrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φίλτρον (phíltron). Unrelated to filtre.

From Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”), from φράζω (phrázō, “to tell, express”).
Learned borrowing from Latin phthisis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek φθίσις (phthísis).

Inherited from Middle French < Old French tisique. Respelled in Middle French to more closely match the Latin phthisicus (with the pronunciation changing to reflect the spelling). By surface analysis, phtisie + -ique.

Inherited from Middle French piller, from Old French pillier, derived from Latin pilleus.

Borrowed from Latin pinacotheca, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē).

Inherited from Old French, from Latin plantāre.

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French plus, from Old French plus, from Latin plus.

From Middle French pluvieux, from Old French pluviex (13th c.), from Latin pluviōsus. From Latin pluvia (“rain”) + -o- + mètre.

Abbreviation of post meridiem, from Latin post meridiem.

pois + chiche, from Old French cice (probably altered under the influence of chiche), itself borrowed from Latin cicer. Cf. also Old French ceire, which was inherited.

Learned borrowing from Latin pollen.

From Latin pomum (“fruit”).

Inherited from Middle French porc, from Old French porc, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”).

parole.significato: stage, scenic (of or relating to a theatrical scene)

From Latin scaenographia, from Ancient Greek σκηνογραφία (skēnographía).

Inherited from Old French secret, borrowed from Latin secrētum.

parole.significato: sect (offshoot of a larger religion or denomination, usually and especially one with unorthodox or extreme political an…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin secta.

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sector.

From Latin sēpia, from Ancient Greek σηπία (sēpía).

Inherited from Middle French seigneur, from Old French seignor (oblique form), from Latin seniōrem (compare sire, derived from the nominative form). Doublet of senior.
Inherited from Latin situla. Doublet of situle.

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sentina (“bilge water, hold of a ship, dregs”).

parole.significato: to smell (to have a certain odor)

parole.significato: to be suitable for; to be proper for

parole.significato: September (the ninth month of the Gregorian calendar, following August and preceding October, containing the southward…
